items.title: 1. Perioperative risk prediction tools
items.q: Discuss the role and limitations of risk prediction tools in adult non-cardiac surgery. Which tools would you use in Australia and New Zealand, and how does a tool change your management?
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, "Adult perioperative risk stratification" (Engelbrecht, Khoyratty, Reilly).

### Why use a tool

There is an ethical duty to give the patient an estimate of risk during consent. Tools can also identify patients who need enhanced monitoring, HDU or ICU, and help allocate limited resources. In the SNAP-2 study of 22,631 patients, **clinician judgement was the only documented tool in 79%**, and using a tool alongside judgement improved risk estimation.

### What makes a good tool

It should be simple, validated in the local population, and judged on two measures:

- **Discrimination:** ability to separate patients who die from those who survive (area under the ROC curve).
- **Calibration:** whether predicted risk matches observed risk. Calibration drifts over time and needs periodic **recalibration**.

### Common tools

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| ASA-PS | Not designed as a risk score but widely used; reasonable discrimination for mortality; a component of SORT and nzRISK |
| RCRI | Six-item major cardiac event estimate |
| ACS NSQIP calculator | About 1.4 million US patients, 21 variables, 30-day mortality and morbidity; proprietary; limits when applied to ANZ patients |
| P-POSSUM | Recalibrated mortality model; original POSSUM includes morbidity prediction |
| SORT | Surgical Outcome Risk Tool: 30-day mortality, includes ASA-PS and urgency |
| nzRISK | New Zealand tool predicting mortality to **2 years**, not just 30 days |

### Limitations

- Most tools predict 30-day mortality, but long-term quality of life matters to patients.
- Models can underpredict in a different population; clinicians may adjust the score.
- There is **little evidence that identifying high-risk patients improves outcomes**; the harder task is to show that risk-stratified care changes patient-centred outcomes.

### Applying the result

Use the estimate for informed consent, shared decision making (including whether to proceed), choice of monitoring, and planned postoperative disposition. Add functional capacity and frailty to the numerical score.

### Self-marking checklist

- Gives the consent and resource-allocation rationale
- Quotes that clinician judgement alone is common and a tool adds value
- Distinguishes discrimination from calibration and mentions recalibration
- Names at least four tools with a feature of each (ASA-PS, RCRI, NSQIP, P-POSSUM, SORT, nzRISK)
- Notes nzRISK includes risk to 2 years
- States the limitation that outcome benefit is unproven
- Describes how the result changes consent and disposition

**Audit evidence map:** BB23-risk; periop26. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.

items.title: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.q: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.a:
- Patients are owed an estimate of risk during consent.
- Tools help target HDU or ICU and limited resources.
- SNAP-2 (22,631 patients): judgement was the only documented tool in 79%.
- Judgement plus a tool estimates risk better than judgement alone.

> **Closing point:** Use a tool to support, not replace, judgement.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.q: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.a:
- Discrimination: separates patients with and without the outcome (AUROC).
- Calibration: predicted risk matches observed risk.
- Calibration drifts, so tools need periodic recalibration.
- Little evidence yet that risk stratification itself improves outcomes.

> **Closing point:** A good AUROC can still give the wrong absolute risk.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.q: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.a:
- ASA-PS: not designed as a score but discriminates mortality well; part of SORT and nzRISK.
- RCRI: six-item cardiac risk.
- ACS NSQIP: 21 variables from about 1.4 million US patients; 30-day mortality and morbidity.
- P-POSSUM and SORT: 30-day mortality.
- nzRISK: New Zealand tool predicting mortality to 2 years.

> **Closing point:** Most tools stop at 30 days; nzRISK looks to 2 years.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.q: Evaluate the use of each of the following for preoperative cardiac risk stratification: • plasma biomarkers (chose ONE of natriuretic peptides OR troponin) • Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) stair-climbing test • cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPX/CPET).
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Evaluate advantages, limitations and evidence for each modality; connect tests to background and procedural risk. The original report itself runs DASI and stair-climbing together (visually checked): both are addressed separately here.

### Put testing in a decision pathway
First define urgency, active unstable cardiac conditions, procedure stress and background risk. A test is useful if it changes shared decision-making, optimisation or postoperative surveillance. Predicting events does not prove that testing itself improves outcome. For the biomarker option I choose **natriuretic peptides**.

### Natriuretic peptides
BNP/NT-proBNP reflect myocardial wall stress and predict perioperative cardiac events beyond clinical risk factors. They are objective, inexpensive and feasible when exercise is limited; a low result may support proceeding without more testing in an otherwise suitable patient. Elevated values can prompt HF/valve assessment and targeted troponin surveillance.

Limitations: age, AF and renal dysfunction raise concentrations; obesity may lower them. An elevated result does not diagnose coronary stenosis, mandate angiography or define an automatic cancellation threshold. Use assay/guideline-specific decision thresholds and symptoms. Evidence is stronger for prognostic association than benefit from a particular biomarker-triggered intervention. A troponin-based answer is an acceptable alternative, but do not spend the answer on two biomarkers when asked to choose one.

### DASI
A structured 12-item self-report of activities estimates functional capacity (score 0–58.2). It is more reproducible than a vague clinician estimate and can be done remotely. METS supports its prognostic usefulness; a score around **≤34** is commonly used to flag poor functional capacity in the perioperative pathway.

It remains self-reported, affected by comprehension, cultural/activity differences and noncardiac disability, and does not localise disease or replace clinical assessment. The score of 34 is a risk decision aid, not a universal “unfit” boundary or the same as directly measured 4 METs.

### Stair climbing
Cheap, accessible integrated exercise assessment: record actual flights/height, pace, symptoms and whether stopping reflects dyspnoea, angina or joint pain. It may expose limitations missed in a history. Protocols and workloads are poorly standardised; frailty, arthritis and claudication confound performance. It cannot quantify gas exchange or exclude CAD and should not provoke exercise in active ACS or another contraindication.

### CPET
A supervised incremental test measures oxygen uptake, anaerobic threshold, peak VO2 and ventilatory efficiency, allowing objective integrated reserve assessment and sometimes identification of cardiac versus ventilatory limitation. It may guide prehabilitation, alternatives and postoperative destination in major surgery.

Cost, equipment, staff, scheduling, contraindications and inability to exercise limit access. Results are effort/protocol dependent; anaerobic-threshold values such as 11 mL/kg/min are population-specific associations, not a universal cancellation rule. A reassuring test cannot remove risk from active disease, and improved risk discrimination does not alone establish improved clinical outcomes.

### Overall judgement
Combine a validated clinical score, structured capacity assessment, frailty and selective testing. Discuss what each result will change before ordering it; emergency surgery usually requires focused assessment and parallel optimisation rather than a full elective testing sequence.

items.q: The Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity (POSSUM) and the Surgical Outcome Risk Tool (SORT) are examples of risk scoring systems used for predicting post-operative morbidity and mortality. Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of these types of risk scoring systems in clinical practice.
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Evaluate usefulness, shared decisions and planning against limits in individuals and local populations; naming scores alone does not answer the question.

### What the tools estimate
POSSUM combines physiological and operative variables to estimate morbidity/mortality; P-POSSUM recalibrates mortality. SORT uses preoperative variables to estimate 30-day mortality. RCRI estimates specified cardiac outcomes, not all postoperative morbidity. Define the outcome/time horizon and use a tool validated for the actual population/procedure.

### Strengths
A transparent estimate complements clinical judgement, supports patient/surgeon discussion about benefit, alternatives and harm, and helps plan optimisation, surgical approach and postoperative care. Standardised recording facilitates audit, case-mix comparison and resource planning. Preoperative tools such as SORT are feasible before the operation; a locally validated tool such as nzRISK can add longer-term mortality estimates.

### Weaknesses and appraisal
Group probabilities cannot predict whether an individual will have an event. **Discrimination** separates event from nonevent; **calibration** compares predicted with observed risk. A high AUROC can coexist with poor absolute estimates. Case mix, geography, ethnicity, procedure changes and improved care can impair transportability or calibration; missing data and subjective inputs add error. POSSUM needs operative details that may be unknown when consent is obtained, and original models may overpredict in contemporary low-risk practice.

Scores may omit frailty, cognition, function, severity of a recent cardiac event and outcomes important to the patient, including independence and quality of life. Apparent risk can influence access to surgery and case selection, complicating comparisons. Predictive accuracy is not evidence that score-triggered care improves survival; avoid false precision or automatic exclusion.

### Practical conclusion
Combine an appropriate locally calibrated tool with structured functional/frailty assessment, active disease, procedure urgency and patient priorities. Explain uncertainty in understandable absolute terms, document what the result changes and reassess when the clinical situation changes. A risk estimate supports a decision; it is not “cardiac clearance”.

items.q: Discuss the usefulness of the ASA grading as a measure of perioperative risk.
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Discuss usefulness on both sides and the emergency modifier; reproducing the full ASA classification is unnecessary and errors in it lose clarity. Remuneration is irrelevant.

### Purpose and usefulness
ASA physical status describes the patient's pre-anaesthetic burden of disease. It is quick, familiar and available without laboratory testing or operative details, improves communication and correlates with postoperative complications and mortality at a population level. It is useful for audit/case mix and is an input in multivariable risk models such as SORT and nzRISK.

### Limits
ASA grade is **not a complete perioperative risk score**: it does not independently specify procedure severity, surgical technique, anaesthetic difficulty, frailty or patient priorities. An ASA II patient having emergency major vascular surgery may have greater risk than an ASA III patient having a minor procedure. Categories are broad, assignment varies between clinicians and examples do not eliminate inter-rater variation. Correlation with mortality does not provide a precise individual percentage or establish that grading improves outcomes.

The **E modifier** denotes emergency surgery where delay significantly increases threat to life or body part; urgency contributes additional risk and should not be ignored or reduced to an arbitrary extra numeric grade. Record both physical status and emergency status, plus the actual disease and operation. If describing the grades, distinguish a healthy patient (I), mild systemic disease (II), severe systemic disease (III), severe disease with constant threat to life (IV), moribund not expected to survive without surgery (V), and declared brain-dead organ donor (VI).

### Conclusion
Use ASA for concise communication and as one component of assessment, supplementing it with urgency, operation, functional reserve/frailty and an appropriately validated risk model. Discuss limitations when counselling an individual rather than presenting an ASA label as a prediction of their outcome.
